title: Why Strength Training Matters
hook: Cardio gets the glory, but lifting, resistance bands, and bodyweight moves protect something running can't: the muscle and bone you'll rely on for decades.
key_points: Adults should do muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days a week.
Strength work preserves muscle and bone that otherwise decline with age.
It improves balance and everyday function, lowering the risk of falls later in life.
Bodyweight, resistance bands, and heavy chores count — you don't need a gym.
content_html: Most people picture jogging when they think "exercise." But the guidelines are just as firm about a second kind of activity: working your muscles against resistance, at least twice a week.
extra_html: The CDC recommends that adults add muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days each week, targeting all the major muscle groups — legs, hips, back, chest, abdomen, shoulders, and arms. This doesn't require a gym: lifting weights, using resistance bands, doing push-ups or squats, and even heavy gardening all count. The payoff is distinct from cardio. Strength work helps maintain the muscle mass and bone density that naturally erode with age, supports a healthy metabolism, and keeps you steady on your feet — a major factor in preventing the falls that become dangerous later in life. Paired with aerobic activity, it rounds out a routine that keeps you not just healthier, but more capable.

source.name: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

related.title: How Much Exercise You Actually Need
related.hook: The headline number is smaller than most people fear: about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — roughly 20-some minutes a day — moves the needle on your health.

related.title: Staying Strong as You Age
related.hook: The decline we associate with old age is partly the result of doing less. Staying active — in four distinct ways — keeps you independent far longer.

related.title: Protecting Your Bones
related.hook: Bone looks permanent, but it's living tissue that thins with age. Osteoporosis weakens it silently until a minor fall causes a major break.

related.title: The Strength-Training Sweet Spot for a Longer Life
related.hook: A 30-year study of 147,000 people points to a modest target: about 90–120 minutes of strength training a week was linked to the biggest drop in risk of dying.

flashcards.explanation_html: CDC guidelines call for muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days a week, working all the major muscle groups.
